Empirical Research Plan – Stock-market Reaction to Monetary-policy Surprises, 1989–2002

------------------------------------------------------------
1. Identification Strategy
------------------------------------------------------------
Method: High-frequency event study with cross-sectional regression of abnormal equity returns on the ex-ante monetary-policy surprise.

Why it is appropriate
•  The research question is: “What happens to stock prices immediately after an unexpected FOMC action?”  
•  Equity markets are assumed to be (approximately) informationally efficient at the daily frequency; therefore the causal effect of new public information can be isolated in a very narrow time window around the announcement (±1 trading day).  
•  The futures-implied surprise is continuously priced until the afternoon of the meeting; the difference between the announced target change and the futures-implied change is therefore exogenous from the point of view of investors on day t–1.  
•  At the aggregate level we estimate β in  
          Abnormal Return_it = α + β Surprise_t + ε_it  
   where i indexes the market, industry, or stock.  
•  For heterogeneity, a difference-in-differences variant compares “interest-sensitive” industries (banks, utilities, durables) to “rate-insensitive” industries (consumer staples, health care). The interaction Surprise_t × Sensitive_i yields a DID estimate of differential effects.

------------------------------------------------------------
2. Treatment and Control
------------------------------------------------------------
Treatment variable  
  Surprise_t ≡ ΔTarget_t  –  ΔFutures_t-1    (in basis points; sign convention: + if the actual rate is higher than expected, i.e., a contractionary surprise).

Control (counterfactual)  
  The return that would have prevailed absent the surprise, proxied by:  
     a) Returns on non-event days (time-series normal-return model), and  
     b) The expected component of the rate change (ΔFutures_t-1) on the same day.

Event date / timing  
  Day 0 = FOMC announcement date. Baseline window: [0] (close-to-close) or [–1,0] to absorb any leakages; robustness windows [0,+1] and intraday (if TAQ later used).  

No running variable or cutoff (not an RDD).

------------------------------------------------------------
3. Key Identifying Assumptions
------------------------------------------------------------
A1 Efficient-market (semi-strong) assumption  
     All publicly available information—including the expected component of the rate change—is already incorporated in prices by the close of t–1.  
     Plausibility: Very high for U.S. equity markets in 1989–2002.

A2 Narrow-window independence  
     In the 1-day window, no other systematic news is correlated with Surprise_t.  
     Plausibility: Reasonable; macro releases are generally not scheduled for 2:15 pm on FOMC days, but we will check calendars.

A3 Accurate measure of expectations  
     Fed funds futures on t–1 provide an unbiased forecast of ΔTarget_t.  
     Plausibility: Supported by prior microstructure evidence; small measurement error remains.

A4 Linearity and stable return-generating process  
     Abnormal returns respond linearly (first-order) to small surprises; non-policy factors are orthogonal.  
     Plausibility: Acceptable over short windows.

------------------------------------------------------------
4. Threats to Identification and Mitigation
------------------------------------------------------------
T1 Concurrent macro announcements (confounders)  
        Mitigation:  i) Drop any events that coincide with major scheduled data releases (Employment Report, CPI, GDP advance, etc.);  
                     ii) Use intraday 2-hour window (12:00–16:00) in a robustness test if TAQ can be added.

T2 Anticipatory trading / information leakage  
        Mitigation:  Include day –1 return in the specification; conduct pre-event placebo test (Surprise_t predicting returns on –2 or –3). No significant coefficient ⇒ limited leakage.

T3 Measurement error in futures-implied expectations  
        Mitigation:  Use alternative contracts (next-month, current-month weighted average) as instruments for Surprise_t; errors-in-variables bias will attenuate β, so we report IV estimates as robustness.

------------------------------------------------------------
5. R Code Outline
------------------------------------------------------------
```r
############################
# 0. Packages -------------
############################
library(data.table)   # fast data handling
library(fixest)       # fast regression
library(lubridate)
library(sandwich)
library(modelsummary)

############################
# 1. Load Data ------------
############################
crsp <- fread("crsp_daily.csv")          # date, vwret (in %), permno, ret, ind17
fomc <- fread("fomc_announcements.csv")  # date, d_target_bp, d_futures_bp

############################
# 2. Merge & Construct ----
############################
crsp[, date := ymd(date)]
fomc[, date := ymd(date)]

# Market-level dataset
mkt <- crsp[, .(vwret = unique(vwret)), by = date]
mkt <- merge(mkt, fomc, by = "date", all.x = TRUE)

# Surprise variable
mkt[, surprise_bp := d_target_bp - d_futures_bp]          # in b.p.
mkt[, surprise := surprise_bp / 100]                      # convert to percentage pts

# Event indicators
mkt[, event_day := !is.na(surprise)]
mkt[, lead1 := shift(event_day, +1)]
mkt[, lag1  := shift(event_day, -1)]

############################
# 3. Main Specification ----
############################
# Abnormal return = raw minus average non-event return
avg_nonevent <- mkt[!event_day, mean(vwret)]
mkt[, abret := vwret - avg_nonevent]

# Regression: event window [-1,0,+1]
sample <- mkt[event_day | lead1 | lag1]

reg1 <- feols(abret ~ surprise, data = sample, vcov = "hetero")
summary(reg1)

############################
# 4. Industry DID ---------
############################
# tag interest-sensitive industries
sensitive_codes <- c(2,4,6,7,11)  # example Fama-French 17 codes
crsp[, sensitive := ind17 %in% sensitive_codes]

# Merge surprise onto stock-level data
crsp <- merge(crsp, fomc[, .(date, surprise)], by = "date", all.x = TRUE)

crsp[, event_day := !is.na(surprise)]
crsp[, abret := ret - mean(ret[!event_day], na.rm = TRUE), by = permno]

did <- feols(abret ~ surprise * sensitive, 
             data = crsp[event_day], 
             cluster = ~date)        # cluster at announcement level
etable(did)

############################
# 5. Robustness: Placebo --
############################
placebo <- feols(lag(abret, 2) ~ surprise, data = mkt[event_day], vcov = "hetero")
etable(reg1, placebo, dict = c(surprise = "Surprise (b.p./100)"))
```

------------------------------------------------------------
6. Expected Results
------------------------------------------------------------
Direction: Contractionary surprises (positive Surprise_t) should reduce equity prices ⇒ β < 0.  
Magnitude (back-of-the-envelope): Prior literature and discount-rate arithmetic suggest roughly –4 to –6 bp on the market per unexpected +1 bp in the funds rate. Thus a +25 bp surprise → about –1.0 % daily abnormal return.

Heterogeneity: Interest-sensitive industries (banks, utilities, durable producers) should decline 30 % more than non-sensitive sectors.

------------------------------------------------------------
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment
(1 = clearly satisfied; 0 = questionable)
------------------------------------------------------------
C1  Clearly defined, narrow event window ………………… 1  
C2  No simultaneous confounding events …………………… 0.7  
C3  Accurate measure of expectations …………………… 0.8  
C4  Efficient-markets assumption ………………………… 0.9  
C5  Correct functional form / linearity ………………… 0.8  

Sum = 4.2 / 5 ⇒ Overall validity judged “high but not bullet-proof.”

------------------------------------------------------------
End of Plan
